analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of oil companies' windfall profits and sends households a $450 rebate.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced with no cosponsors in December 2005, it was referred to committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged integrated oil companies an excise tax equal to 50% of their 'windfall profit' on crude oil sold during 2005 — the amount by which the sale price of a barrel exceeded a $40 base price. The revenue would fund a one-time $450 rebate, paid by March 1, 2006, to individual taxpayers whose prior-year income was $40,000 or less. Oil companies could deduct the tax from their income taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: About 43 million individual taxpayers earning $40,000 or less would have each received a $450 rebate check by March 1, 2006, funded entirely by a new tax on integrated oil companies' excess 2005 profits.

how_it_helps.text: Each eligible taxpayer would be treated as having paid $450 toward their taxes and remitted that amount by March 1, 2006 [S3].
Eligibility was limited to taxpayers with adjusted gross income of $40,000 or less in the prior year, excluding dependents claimed by others, estates and trusts, and nonresident aliens [S2] [S3].

The tax applied to 50% of the profit above a $40-per-barrel base price on crude oil sold in 2005 by integrated oil companies, so the rebate was funded by the industry rather than by general taxpayers [S2] [S3].
The tax excluded oil from wells drilled after enactment, a design meant to avoid discouraging new drilling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies — large firms that both produce and refine crude oil — would pay an excise tax of 50% of windfall profits on 2005 crude sales. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers at the pump, though the tax was temporary and applied only to 2005 taxable years.

drawbacks.text: The tax was limited to integrated oil companies and 2005 taxable years, so non-integrated producers and future profits were untouched, limiting how much revenue it could raise [S2] [S3].

A tax on producers can be passed through to consumers in higher fuel prices, and economists have long debated whether windfall profits taxes discourage future investment in supply; the bill's exclusion of newly drilled wells only partly addressed that [S3].
The rebate was a one-time $450 payment, not a lasting fix for energy costs, and it phased out entirely at $40,000 of income, excluding many working households just above that line [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit — $450 to tens of millions of lower- and middle-income households during a period of high gasoline and heating prices — outweighed the drawbacks for those households, since the cost fell on oil companies' excess 2005 profits. The design limits were real: it was a one-time payment, the income cutoff excluded households just above $40,000, and some portion of the tax might have been passed through to fuel prices. But the bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Lieberman introduced the bill on December 14, 2005, with Sen. Reid introducing it on his behalf [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which had jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies kept their excess 2005 profits untaxed, since no comparable windfall tax was enacted. Lower-income households never received the $450 rebate. The Senate Finance Committee, as the gatekeeper that declined to act, avoided taking any recorded position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Integrated oil companies, which avoided the tax

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the windfall profits tax and household rebate bill; drew no cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.role: Senator (NV), introduced the bill on Lieberman's behalf
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate for Sen. Lieberman.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 14, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-controlled Senate committee never took it up, so no vote ever revealed where members stood.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed 50% of their 2005 windfall profits above $40 per barrel of crude, with the proceeds going to household rebates. Their financial interest ran directly against the rebate's beneficiaries, and the bill's death left their excess profits untaxed. [S2] [S3]
The tax applied only to integrated oil companies, so independent producers were spared the tax while still selling into the same high-price market. [S2] [S3]
